Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the About page for a company that makes scheduling software for medical clinics. Around 250 words.

About Us

Meridian Health builds scheduling software for medical clinics. We started after watching a friend's practice run three separate systems — one for booking, one for reminders, one for provider calendars — none of which talked to each other. Front desk staff spent their mornings reconciling double bookings by hand.

Our platform handles the whole scheduling flow: patient booking, provider availability, room and equipment assignment, and automated reminders that cut no-show rates. It works for a single-physician practice and for a multi-site clinic group with shared resources across locations. Everything syncs in real time, so a change made at the front desk shows up instantly on a provider's tablet.

We built the system around a few constraints clinics told us mattered most. It has to work when the internet connection drops, so the local view keeps functioning and syncs once the connection returns. It has to meet HIPAA requirements without extra configuration, so encryption and audit logs are on by default. And it has to be usable by staff who have five minutes of training, not five hours.

The team includes former clinic administrators, schedulers, and engineers who spent years building systems for hospitals before deciding to focus on the smaller practices that hospital software ignores. We test every feature with real front desk staff before it ships, because a scheduling tool that confuses the person using it fails, regardless of what it can do on paper.

Today, clinics in over 30 states use Meridian Health to manage appointments for several million patients. We keep building based on what staff tell us they need, one clinic at a time.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.
